extracted.intended_audience: EPO patent attorneys, oppositions practitioners, patentees and other IP professionals interested in European patent prosecution and opposition practice
extracted.subtask_short: amending patent description to match claims
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether and when the description of a European patent (or application) must be adapted to remove inconsistencies with claims amended during opposition or examination proceedings, and what legal provisions (if any) require such adaptation. Focuses on EPO case law, procedural stages (opposition vs examination) and the referral G 1/25 to the Enlarged Board of Appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity to adapt the description to amended claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claims of a European patent are amended during opposition or examination proceedings and the amendment introduces an inconsistency between the amended claims and the description, is it necessary, to comply with the requirements of the EPC, to adapt the description to the amended claims so as to remove the inconsistency?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common practice before the EPO is to adapt the description (often at the end of opposition proceedings) so it is in line with the maintained/amended claims. The article frames this as the central question referred to the Enlarged Board of Appeal in G 1/25 and gives the practical example of a description that still discloses embodiments that fall outside the scope of newly-limited claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal basis — Article 84 EPC (clarity/support) as a ground for adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: One line of case law derives a need to adapt the description from Article 84 EPC, i.e. requirements of clarity and support of the claims in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some Boards have treated Article 84 (alone or combined with other provisions) as providing the requisite legal basis for requiring adaptation of the description where inconsistencies arise. The article notes this is the more commonly-followed line of case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal basis — Rule 42 EPC (content of the description) as a ground for adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 42 EPC (content of the description) is cited in case law as another provision supporting adaptation of the description to match amended claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 42 has been used (sometimes together with Article 84) to justify amending the description so that it does not describe embodiments outside the scope of the maintained claims. The article lists Rule 42 as among the sources invoked by the traditional approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative line of authority — no legal basis for requiring adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: A recent line of decisions (notably in examination-appeal proceedings) holds there is no legal basis in the EPC to require adaptation of the description to fit amended claims, rejecting Article 84 and other provisions as providing such a basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These 'radical' decisions challenge the traditional practice. The article highlights this divergence in case law as motivating the referral G 1/25. Practitioners should be aware of these decisions when advising clients, particularly in examination-appeal contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural-context distinction — opposition vs examination proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the requirement (if any) to adapt the description depends on whether the claims were amended during opposition/opposition-appeal proceedings or during examination/examination-appeal proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The referral explicitly asks whether the answer to the adaptation question would be different in examination proceedings. The article notes that some recent case law that denies a requirement has arisen in examination-appeal proceedings, suggesting potential divergence by procedural stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common practice and timing for description adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice, descriptions are usually adapted to the maintained/amended claims at the end of opposition proceedings, and similarly during later stages of examination where claims are amended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states this is routine practice: to amend the description so it does not disclose embodiments that are outside the scope of the allowed/maintained claims. This pragmatic timing (typically at the conclusion of proceedings) is important for docketing and client advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances that give rise to inconsistency between claims and description
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconsistency arises where amended (usually narrowed) claims exclude embodiments that the original description continues to disclose, for example where the description indicates the invention includes embodiments that are no longer within the scope of the maintained claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying such passages is the first step: if the description still describes features/embodiments broader than the amended claims, practitioners commonly consider adapting or deleting those passages to avoid inconsistency. The article uses the example from T 0697/22 involving a narrower definition of an 'organic binder' in the maintained claims than in the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of an inconsistent description on claim interpretation (UPC authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Case law (e.g., UPC Hamburg decision AGFA NV v Gucci Sweden AB) has held that a broader description inconsistent with maintained claims cannot be used to interpret more limited claims to the patentee's benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indicates that, at least in some courts, an inconsistent description will not expand claim scope; however, the treatment of such inconsistencies varies and does not resolve whether adaptation is required under the EPC. Practitioners should consider both national/court authority and EPO practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral questions to the Enlarged Board of Appeal (G 1/25)
rubrics_metrics.description: The referral G 1/25 poses three specific questions: (1) is it necessary under the EPC to adapt the description to amended claims after amendments create inconsistency; (2) if so, which EPC provision(s) necessitate such adaptation; (3) would the answers differ if the amendment occurred during examination/examination-appeal proceedings?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The outcome of these questions will determine whether the traditional practice continues to be legally required or whether the more recent decisions denying a legal basis prevail. The article highlights that the Enlarged Board's decision will be decisive for boards' and departments' practice at the EPO.
